purpose: Mepolizumab is used to help control severe asthma that is not well managed with regular inhalers, especially a type called eosinophilic asthma. It is also used to treat other conditions involving too many eosinophils (a type of white blood cell) in the body, such as certain nasal polyp conditions and rare blood disorders. It helps reduce flare-ups and makes breathing easier over time.
how_it_works: Your body makes a protein called IL-5 that tells certain white blood cells called eosinophils to grow and cause inflammation in your airways. Mepolizumab blocks that IL-5 protein so fewer eosinophils are produced. With less inflammation, your airways stay calmer and your asthma symptoms improve.
common_side_effects: Headache, back pain, tiredness, injection site reactions like redness or swelling, and upper respiratory infections such as a cold or sore throat are the most commonly reported side effects.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have a parasitic infection before starting this medication, as it may make it harder for your body to fight certain worms. Do not suddenly stop your other asthma medicines without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel better. Rarely, serious allergic reactions can occur, usually within hours of the injection, so watch for rash, swelling, or trouble breathing and seek help immediately. This medicine is given as an injection under the skin every 4 weeks by a healthcare provider or trained caregiver.
typical_dosing: The usual dose for adults and children 12 and older with severe asthma is 100 mg injected under the skin once every 4 weeks. For children 6 to 11 years old with asthma, the dose is 40 mg every 4 weeks. Dosing may differ for other conditions. Injections are typically given in the upper arm, thigh, or belly area.
